title: Generics
summary: Write one method or class that works for every type, without giving up type safety.

steps.title: One method, many types
body: You have used `List<int>` and `List<string>`. The `<...>` part is a **generic type argument**. Now you will write the other side: code that *accepts* one.
Without generics you would copy the same method once per type:
```csharp
static int LastInt(List<int> items) => items[items.Count - 1];
static string LastString(List<string> items) => items[items.Count - 1];
The bodies are identical. Only the type changes. A **generic method** turns the type into a parameter:
```csharp
static T Last<T>(List<T> items) => items[items.Count - 1];
- `<T>` after the method name declares a **type parameter**. `T` is a placeholder.
- Everywhere else, `T` is used like a normal type.
- The caller decides what `T` is: `Last<int>(numbers)` or `Last<string>(names)`.
> **Tip:** You could use `object` instead, but then the caller gets an `object` back and has to cast. Generics keep the real type, so mistakes are caught by the compiler.

steps.prompt: Complete the generic method. It builds a list that holds `value` repeated `count` times, for any type.
code: static List<T> Repeat__1__(__2__ value, int count)
steps.explain: `<T>` after the name declares the type parameter. After that, `T` is used wherever the real type would go.

steps.title: Type inference
body: You rarely have to write the type argument. The compiler works it out from the arguments you pass. This is called **type inference**.
```csharp
var prices = new List<decimal> { 4.50m, 9.99m };
decimal a = Last<decimal>(prices);   // explicit
decimal b = Last(prices);            // inferred: T is decimal
Inside a generic method, `typeof(T)` tells you which type was chosen for this call.

steps.prompt: What does this program print? (`typeof(int).Name` is `Int32`, `typeof(string).Name` is `String`, `typeof(double).Name` is `Double`.)
steps.explain: For the first two calls `T` is inferred from the argument. The third call says `T` is `double` explicitly, so the `3` is converted to a `double`.

steps.title: Make them generic
prompt: These two methods only work for `int`. Make both generic so they work for **any** type.
- `static T FirstOr<T>(List<T> items, T fallback)` returns the first item, or `fallback` when the list is empty.
- `static List<T> Reversed<T>(List<T> items)` returns a **new** list with the items in reverse order. The original list must not change.
```csharp
FirstOr(new List<string>(), "none")          // "none"
Reversed(new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 })           // 3, 2, 1
Write the loop for `Reversed` yourself; do not call the built-in `Reverse`.
starter: // Replace int with a type parameter so both methods work for any type.
static int FirstOr(List<int> items, int fallback)
solution: static T FirstOr<T>(List<T> items, T fallback)
template: Dojo.Eq("FirstOr returns the first int", 7, FirstOr(new List<int> { 7, 8 }, -1));
Dojo.Eq("FirstOr returns the fallback for an empty list", -1, FirstOr(new List<int>(), -1));
Dojo.Eq("FirstOr works for strings", "none", FirstOr(new List<string>(), "none"));
Dojo.Eq("Reversed(1, 2, 3) is 3, 2, 1", new List<int> { 3, 2, 1 }, Reversed(new List<int> { 1, 2, 3 }));
Dojo.Eq("Reversed works for strings", new List<string> { "c", "b", "a" }, Reversed(new List<string> { "a", "b", "c" }));
Dojo.Eq("Reversed leaves the original list unchanged", new List<int> { 1, 2 }, original);

forbid.message: Does not call the built-in Reverse

hints: Put `<T>` right after each method name, then replace every `int` that means "the item type" with `T`. The loop counter stays an `int`.
`Reversed`: create `new List<T>()`, loop `i` from `items.Count - 1` down to `0`, and `Add(items[i])`.

steps.title: Generic classes
body: A class can take type parameters too. That is how `List<T>` and `Dictionary<TKey, TValue>` are built.
```csharp
class Page<T>
public int Number { get; }
public List<T> Items { get; }
public Page(int number, List<T> items)
Number = number;
Items = items;
var page = new Page<string>(1, new List<string> { "Ann", "Bo" });
string first = page.Items[0];   // a string, no cast
The type parameter goes after the **class** name. Every member can then use `T`. `Page<string>` and `Page<Order>` are two different types made from one piece of code.
You can have more than one parameter: `class Pair<TFirst, TSecond>`. When there are several, give them descriptive names that start with `T`.

steps.prompt: Arrange the lines into a generic class that stores one value, set through its constructor.
steps.explain: The class declares `T` once, after its name. The property type and the constructor parameter both reuse it. (The property may also come after the constructor; members can be in any order.)

steps.title: RecentList<T>
prompt: A search box shows the last few things you searched for. Write a generic class `RecentList<T>` that keeps only the most recent items.
- Constructor `RecentList(int capacity)`: the most items it will hold.
- `void Add(T item)`: adds an item. If that makes the list longer than `capacity`, the **oldest** item is dropped.
- `int Count`: how many items it holds now.
- `IReadOnlyList<T> Items`: the items, oldest first.
```csharp
var recent = new RecentList<string>(2);
recent.Add("tea"); recent.Add("mug"); recent.Add("pot");
// recent.Items is "mug", "pot"
starter: // a private List<T> is a good place to keep the items
template: Dojo.Eq("a new RecentList is empty", 0, recent.Count);
Dojo.Eq("Count is 2 after two adds", 2, recent.Count);
Dojo.Eq<IEnumerable<string>>("Items are oldest first", new[] { "tea", "mug" }, recent.Items);
Dojo.Eq("Count never goes above the capacity", 3, recent.Count);
Dojo.Eq<IEnumerable<string>>("the oldest item was dropped", new[] { "mug", "pot", "cup" }, recent.Items);
hints: Keep two private fields: a `List<T>` for the items and an `int` for the capacity. The constructor stores the capacity.
`Count` and `Items` can just forward to the inner list: `_items.Count` and `_items`.
In `Add`: add the item, then `if (_items.Count > _capacity) _items.RemoveAt(0);`. Index 0 is the oldest.

steps.title: Constraints
body: Inside a generic method the compiler knows nothing about `T`. It could be anything, so you can only do what works for *every* type. This does not compile:
```csharp
static T Max<T>(T a, T b) => a > b ? a : b;   // error: > is not defined for T
A **constraint** narrows what `T` may be. In return you may use what that kind of type offers:
```csharp
static T Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>
=> a.CompareTo(b) > 0 ? a : b;
`int`, `string`, `decimal` and `DateTime` all implement `IComparable<T>`. `a.CompareTo(b)` is positive when `a` is larger, zero when equal, negative when smaller.
| Constraint | `T` must be | You may then |
| `where T : IComparable<T>` | comparable to itself | call `CompareTo` |
| `where T : class` | a reference type | use `null` |
| `where T : struct` | a value type | rely on it never being `null` |
| `where T : new()` | a type with a parameterless constructor | write `new T()` |
| `where T : Employee` | `Employee` or a subclass | use `Employee` members |

steps.prompt: Match each constraint to what it lets you write inside the method.
steps.explain: A constraint is a promise from the caller. The compiler then lets the method rely on that promise.

prompt: Given this method, which calls compile?
```csharp
static T Max<T>(T a, T b) where T : IComparable<T>
=> a.CompareTo(b) > 0 ? a : b;
steps.explain: `int`, `string` and `decimal` implement `IComparable<T>`. `object` and `List<int>` do not, so the constraint rejects them. `Max(3, "nine")` fails earlier: there is no single `T` that is both `int` and `string`.

steps.title: Missing constraints
prompt: Neither method compiles, because each one does something that is not possible for *every* `T`.
- `Largest<T>(List<T> items)` should return the largest item in a non-empty list.
- `CreateMany<T>(int count)` should return a list of `count` brand-new `T` objects.
Add the right constraint to each method, and change the comparison so it uses what the constraint gives you.
solution: static T Largest<T>(List<T> items) where T : IComparable<T>
static List<T> CreateMany<T>(int count) where T : new()
template: Dojo.Eq("Largest of pear, apple, plum is plum", "plum", Largest(new List<string> { "pear", "apple", "plum" }));
Dojo.Check("every created Ticket is a real new object", CreateMany<Ticket>(2).All(t => t != null && t.Status == "open"), "expected new Ticket objects with Status \"open\"");
class Ticket { public string Status { get; set; } = "open"; }
hints: A constraint goes after the parameter list: `static T Largest<T>(List<T> items) where T : ...`.
`>` does not exist for an unknown `T`. With `where T : IComparable<T>` you can write `item.CompareTo(best) > 0` instead.

steps.title: Sidekick: the top N of anything
prompt: **Sidekick piece.** Sidekick ranks many things: tasks by minutes logged, days by time worked, tags by use. Write the
ranking once, for any type, with a constraint that guarantees the key can be compared.
`static List<T> TopBy<T, TKey>(IEnumerable<T> items, Func<T, TKey> key, int count) where TKey : IComparable<TKey>`
- returns at most `count` items, **highest key first**.
- items with equal keys keep their original order (sort positions, not items, and break ties by position).
- `count` larger than the number of items returns them all; `count` of 0 returns an empty list.
- a negative `count` throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException`.
- do it with a `List<int>` of positions and `Sort` (no LINQ yet).
```text
TopBy(words, w => w.Length, 1)                  -> the longest word (the first one, if several tie)
TopBy(yourTasks, t => t.LoggedMinutes, 2)       -> the two tasks you spent most time on
Your `TaskItem` is ready for the tests.
starter: static List<T> TopBy<T, TKey>(IEnumerable<T> items, Func<T, TKey> key, int count) where TKey : IComparable<TKey>
solution: static List<T> TopBy<T, TKey>(IEnumerable<T> items, Func<T, TKey> key, int count) where TKey : IComparable<TKey>
if (count < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(count), "count cannot be negative.");
for (int i = 0; i < list.Count; i++) order.Add(i);
for (int i = 0; i < order.Count && i < count; i++) top.Add(list[order[i]]);
hints: Copy the items into a `List<T> list`, then make `order` = 0, 1, 2, ... list.Count - 1.
`order.Sort((a, b) => { int c = key(list[b]).CompareTo(key(list[a])); return c != 0 ? c : a.CompareTo(b); });`
Take the first `count` positions and look each one up in `list`.
template: Dojo.Eq("the two highest numbers", new List<int> { 9, 9 }, TopBy(new[] { 3, 9, 1, 9 }, n => n, 2));
Dojo.Eq("ties keep their order", new List<string> { "bb", "cc" }, TopBy(new[] { "a", "bb", "cc", "d" }, w => w.Length, 2));
Dojo.Eq("count larger than the list returns all, sorted", new List<int> { 5, 2, 1 }, TopBy(new[] { 2, 5, 1 }, n => n, 10));
Dojo.Eq("count 0 is empty", new List<int>(), TopBy(new[] { 2, 5, 1 }, n => n, 0));
Dojo.Eq("an empty input is empty", new List<int>(), TopBy(new int[0], n => n, 3));
Dojo.Throws<ArgumentOutOfRangeException>("a negative count throws", () => TopBy(new[] { 1 }, n => n, -1));
Dojo.Eq("works with DateOnly keys", new List<DateOnly> { new(2026, 12, 1) }, TopBy(new[] { new DateOnly(2026, 11, 2), new DateOnly(2026, 12, 1) }, d => d, 1));
var dojoTasks = new List<TaskItem> { new(1, "Docs"), new(2, "Login"), new(3, "Tests") };
Dojo.Eq("your tasks by minutes logged", new List<int> { 2, 3 }, TopBy(dojoTasks, t => t.LoggedMinutes, 2).Select(t => t.Id).ToList());
public TaskItem(int id, string title, int estimateMinutes = 0)
if (id < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(id), "Task ids start at 1.");
if (string.IsNullOrWhiteSpace(title)) throw new ArgumentException("A task needs a title.", nameof(title));
if (estimateMinutes < 0) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(estimateMinutes), "An estimate cannot be negative.");
public int LoggedMinutes { get; private set; }
public bool IsRunning { get; private set; }
public DateTime StartedAt { get; private set; }
public bool Done { get; private set; }
string projectPart = Project is { Length: > 0 } p ? $" @{p}" : "";
string duePart = Due is DateOnly d ? $" (due {d:ddd d MMM})" : "";
if (Done) throw new InvalidOperationException("A finished task cannot be started.");
if (at < StartedAt) throw new ArgumentException("A timer cannot stop before it started.", nameof(at));
if (minutes < 1) throw new ArgumentOutOfRangeException(nameof(minutes), "Log at least one minute.");
steps.explain: `where TKey : IComparable<TKey>` is a promise the compiler checks at every call: you can call `CompareTo` on any key, and nobody can pass a key type that cannot be ordered. One method now ranks ints, dates and your tasks.
